Pele Yoetz 152:6: And then the LORD shall rejoice in His works, and the LORD shall say, "how dear is My son to Me, who is in My world - see how he accepts sufferings and justifies the judgment upon himself," and He shall return and heal him. But if he does not take it to heart and attributes the matter to chance, his judgment is already explicit from the mouth of the Almighty in Parashat Bechukotai, as it is written (Leviticus 26:27-28), "and if you walk with Me casually [by chance], then I too shall walk with you in the fury of chance, and I shall add to chastise you," and so on. And the commentators have already written that "nature" (teva) has the same numerical value as "God" (Elokim), to indicate that everything is under His individual providence, blessed be His Name. And how good it is to make a fence for oneself: when he sees suffering coming upon him, let him accept with all firmness to withdraw his hand from something he is doing that is not good, and to fulfill some good thing he was not doing, and through this he shall be accepted as one who offers a fire-offering sacrifice.
Pele Yoetz 153:1: Treifah [Non-Kosher Meat] - How great are the laws of treifah! Happy is the God-fearing man who can be careful not to eat from an animal that a sage declared treifah, even though the greatest of the greatest halachic authorities validate it - one must still be concerned. And this piety is preferable to every kind of piety in the world, as it is written (Proverbs 23:2), "and put a knife to your throat if you are a man of appetite" - for one must be very careful of any hint of prohibition and be stringent regarding matters touching eating and drinking, for "all of man's labor is for his mouth" (Ecclesiastes 6:7), and if he encounters a prohibition, the body grows on prohibited food and makes his own soul a forbidden morsel, and the spirit of impurity rests upon him, and there is no way or entrance for a holy spirit to rest upon him - and from this, he goes from evil to evil, and cannot understand and comprehend, to hear teaching and to teach, and to intend to fear and love the honored LORD, and to rejoice at a time of gladness, the joy of a mitzvah, and to grieve at a time of sadness, as is proper to do.
Pele Yoetz 153:2: And it is already told of the pious Rabbi Shelah [author of Shnei Luchot HaBrit], that when he took leave of his teacher who taught him wisdom, he asked him to teach him the paths of life by which he would merit the life of the World to Come. And he told him to be careful of three things: to sanctify himself greatly at the time of intercourse, in holiness and purity and pure thoughts, so that the foundation of the offspring not be faulty and built through prohibition, God forbid, which would cause him not to be able to attain the paths of life so well; and likewise to be very careful of prohibited food, so that the body not be built through prohibition; and to flee from a hundred gates of the permitted, so as not to enter one gate of the forbidden. And of such a case they said (Chullin 44b): who is a Torah scholar? Whoever declares an animal treifah for himself - that although he is lenient for others, he is stringent with himself in order to satisfy all opinions.
Pele Yoetz 153:3: And behold, it is difficult to find an animal that is clean of everything bad and that is kosher according to all opinions, and who can stand guard over this? Therefore I found pleasing the custom of pious men and men of deeds, whom I saw, that they would eat only poultry. But the difficult thing is that one must also be able to do this - not to feast in another's home. Happy is the man who does this and is careful of every hint of prohibition in eating and drinking, and he merits the help of Heaven. And the essence of this mitzvah rests upon the ritual slaughterers and upon the halachic decisors - let them tremble and be seized when they come to examine for the prohibition of treifah, and let them learn thoroughly, thoroughly, in examining the lung and in knowing all the laws and all the reasoning, and let them be very afraid and fear God, not to feed treifot to Israel, God forbid, and in a place of doubt or dispute let them go toward stringency, and especially regarding a gentile's money, they should not seek the strength of leniency. This is the straight path.
Pele Yoetz 154:1: Trouble - It is a great principle for the whole of solitary devotion and for all worldly affairs and possessions, that it is impossible to profit without trouble, and according to the greatness of the trouble, so is the greatness of the profit - but against the profit, if it is great, the trouble diminishes into vanity, and on the contrary, it becomes sweet and pleasant. Behold, therefore, whoever reckons the reward of a mitzvah and the profit of giving a person peace of mind to his Former, certainly every kind of trouble and affliction shall be light at the time of weighing, and he shall be alert and rewarded, and let the weak say, "I am mighty," and let him do whatever is in his power to do. Of this it is said (Proverbs 2:4-5), "if you seek it as silver, then you shall understand the fear of the LORD." And just as it must be very light in his own eyes to trouble himself with the trouble of a mitzvah, or in order to profit, correspondingly it must be very heavy for him to trouble others, even the smallest trouble, if there is concern it would be heavy for them. Go out and learn from the mitzvah the Torah commanded (Leviticus 19:32), "you shall rise before gray hair and honor the presence of an elder" - and even so, they said (Kiddushin 33a): whoever goes around [avoiding forcing people to rise] lives longer - that is, one who goes by another route so as not to trouble the people to rise before him. And elsewhere they said in the Midrash (Bamidbar Rabbah 15:17) that it is fitting for a sage to intend to pass before the people so that they rise before him, and they fulfill a mitzvah and give peace of mind to our Former, and receive good reward for their effort. And I say the resolution of the matter is that everything depends on what kind of people they are: if they desire mitzvot and it is no trouble to them, then let him pass before them - but if he suspects that they do not desire the mitzvah and it is a trouble and burden to them, then "whoever goes around lives longer."
Pele Yoetz 154:2: And from this one can also learn a manner of conduct: that a person shall conduct himself with his sons, his wife, and every person - if he sees that they love and desire to serve him in order to fulfill a mitzvah incumbent upon them or out of love of kindness, then let him instruct them to serve him; but if he sees that it is heavy for them because they do not desire the mitzvot, and if they do it out of embarrassment, or because they are subjugated to him and do it against their own will, unwillingly, then he should not trouble them and should not burden them, but shall serve himself with his own dignity. And especially when the members of the household or his servants are asleep, it is fitting to have all the more regard for them, not to wake them from their sleep, but rather he himself shall perform his own needs and their needs, and it shall be counted as a mitzvah to perform kindness with every person, even with his own wife and household members. And everything depends on the time and the season and on the nature and traits of the members of his household - if it would be heavy for them and not heavy for him, better that he trouble himself a little rather than that it be a trouble for them, and let him honor the LORD with what He has graced him, being light on his feet and not lazy, and let him perform kindness with every person.
Pele Yoetz 154:3: But if the matter is very heavy for him, or he needs to neglect the work of Heaven, or it is something he cannot do himself, then he is compelled to trouble others. And what they said (Ketubot 96a), "whoever prevents his student from serving him withholds kindness from him and removes fear of Heaven from him" - this refers to a worthy student who desires to merit mitzvot, in which case it is a mitzvah to bring him merit through such a great mitzvah, whose reward is fear of Heaven, as it is written (Leviticus 19:32), "and you shall honor the presence of an elder and fear your God" - and there is no kindness greater than this. And this applies to every person: if he sees that it is his desire and will to serve him and trouble himself before him, thinking it shall be counted a mitzvah for him and wishing to give peace of mind to his Former, then it is a mitzvah to bring him merit and do his will as he wishes, for a person's own will is his honor, and the honor of Heaven increases, and their reward be praised on high. And in the manner they said (Vayikra Rabbah 34:8), that more than the rich man does for the poor man, the poor man does for the rich man - for the rich man gives a bit of money to the poor man, while the poor man brings him merit for the life of the World to Come. So it is with this matter, that the one served does more good for the servant than the servant does for the one served, for the servant serves a little with his body and merits to give peace of mind to his Former and abundant good. But he should not judge by the appearance of his eyes when someone shows a pleasant face wishing to serve him - one must be concerned lest he does it out of embarrassment, and should not wish nor accept until the matter is clear to him that he does it with a whole heart, because he reckons the reward of a mitzvah and wishes to give peace of mind to his Former. And even this he should not accept from one who studies halachot and is not his student, for they said (Megillah 28a): it is forbidden to make use of one who studies halachot, for there is concern that in any case his mind is weakened by it - only if he does it of his own accord, out of his own will, is it permitted. And if it is something not befitting his own honor and involves disgrace for him, he should not accept it, as they said in the Talmud (ibid.): if you are accustomed to carrying a burden, well and good, but if not, I do not wish to be honored at your expense.
Pele Yoetz 154:4: And it is not only regarding matters of service that one must weigh with a scale and just balances as stated, but the same law applies to any kind of thing one wishes to request from his fellow, and any kind of involvement he has with his fellow - one must be very concerned that it not be a trouble and heavy burden upon him, and treat every person as though they do not desire kindness, and even a minor trouble shall be considered heavy for them as though it were a prolonged trouble. And there are cases where a heavy burden upon others is light for him compared to the reward of a mitzvah. But he should not burden any person at all until the matter is clear to him and he has gotten to the bottom of that person's mind, and then he shall find favor in the eyes of God and man.
Pele Yoetz 155:1: Arguments - Whoever makes false and rejected arguments is hated and detestable in the eyes of God and man, for words of truth are foreign to him, and whoever hears his fellow making false arguments against him, his teeth shall grind, saying, "the living does not deny the living - how are you not ashamed and embarrassed?" And likewise, if he wishes to excuse himself with false and rejected pretexts, let his fellow become angry too, saying, "what do you think - do your friends eat straw, are they like animals, that they do not understand your cunning and your deceit?" - and then his fellow's anger shall be kindled and his wrath shall burn within him, and a flame of division shall rise. And they have already given a sign: "Cozbi, daughter of the prince of Midian" - and "emet" (truth) is the foundation of the building. Go out and learn from the trait of our Maker, as it is written (Jeremiah 2:35), "behold, I shall enter into judgment with you because you say, I have not sinned." And this was the difference between Saul and David: for Saul sought to excuse himself and said (I Samuel 15:9), "for the people spared the best of the flock," and so on, and therefore he was punished with death. But David, who said, "I have sinned," the prophet immediately said to him (II Samuel 12:13), "the LORD has also removed your sin - you shall not die." And behold, it is not necessary to say that it is forbidden to make false arguments, for one transgresses what the Torah said (Exodus 23:7), "keep far from a false matter." But sometimes even true arguments are not good to make if he knows about his fellow that he does not accept an argument - silence is beautiful, or let him say, "truly I have sinned, and I ask forgiveness." So shall the man who seeks peace act.
Pele Yoetz 156:1: Error - There is no person in the world who does not err, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 116:11): "every man is a liar." And it is no shame for a person to say he erred, but to hold fast to his error and say he did not err - this is shame and disgrace. Whichever way you look at it: if he does not recognize his own error, it turns out he is a fool and a boor, as they explained on the verse (ibid. 73:22), "and I was boorish and did not know" - meaning, I did not know that I was boorish, "then behold, I was like a beast" - two things I was. And if he recognizes his own error and is ashamed to admit it and wishes to hold fast to his error, this adds folly and shame to his shame, for words of truth are foreign to him, since he wishes to hold fast to his error with false and rejected pretexts, and everyone who hears shall laugh at him and recognize his bad trait - but he thinks that people do not get to the bottom of his mind and that he can mislead them with his words. And this too is a bad trait in a person, that he is wiser in his own eyes than everyone else - over this the listeners shall grind their teeth: why does he consider them like animals, and why does he have this bad trait of holding fast to his error? But the acknowledgment of the Rabbis is itself their praise. And who is greater than Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, and it is written (Leviticus 10:20), "and Moses heard and it was good in his eyes" - he acknowledged and was not ashamed. And likewise we find firm foundations of the earth who would preach publicly and say, "what I said in your presence is an error on my part" (Shabbat 63b). And even if it seems shameful to him to admit it, better to err in this world and not be ashamed in the World to Come. Therefore let a person be God-fearing and acknowledge the truth, for the honor of the LORD, the God of truth.
Pele Yoetz 157:1: Outing - This too is an inclination in man: that in the days of summer, people increase in taking themselves out to pasture in gardens beneath a leafy tree, on the banks of rivers and streams, and increase there in eating and drinking and reveling with the joy of merrymaking, and some are greatly obsessed with the pleasures and vanities of this world, and they hasten to go before the morning prayer, and neglect communal prayer and the synagogue, and are drawn after excessive eating and drinking until night follows day - and all is vanity and vexation of spirit. And how many transgressions follow from this, as one standing guard shall see at every merrymaking feast, that evil follows evil, and he adds to this by going on an outing, for they said in the Holy Zohar that it is forbidden for us to look at anything that gladdens the heart, for the smoke of the burning of the Temple is upon our eyes.
Pele Yoetz 157:2: And there is already room for exemption and a bit of a mitzvah to go on an outing - such as if he is sick with melancholy, or is sad and his heart is dulled, he may go on a small outing once in a great while with two or three jesting men, to a place that broadens a person's heart, so that he forget his sadness and his heart be greatly broadened, and then he shall return promptly to Torah study, and be able to understand and comprehend and serve his Creator with complete service while he is healthy - however, in a manner that his deeds be for the sake of Heaven, then perhaps the LORD shall count it as a mitzvah for him, provided there is no hint of prohibition and no lack of mitzvah observance there. But the complete man, who cleaves to the LORD with great love, shall despise all these, and shall not find greater tranquility of spirit, a good outing, and great pleasure than in sitting in the study house, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said: the study house is an orchard for the righteous and a prison for the wicked. But whoever is not so attached to the LORD, it is a necessity for him from time to time to give a portion and do a bit of his inclination's will specifically for the honor of his Maker - and this is a matter entrusted to the heart, and God shall search out this and similar matters, for He knows the secrets of the heart.
Pele Yoetz 158:1: Purity - Purity brings a person to everything in holiness, for it is known that the will of the Israelite soul is to fear and love the honored and awesome Name and to cleave to Him and to serve Him with complete service and fulfill all the mitzvot as is proper to do, at a time of gladness - gladness, joy, and happiness shall be found in it, and at a time of sadness, an eye shall weep bitterly and sigh in bitterness with a broken and crushed heart, as is proper to do. But what shall the man do whose heart is not in his own hand, and who cannot do the will of his Father in Heaven as he wishes, and whose heart is not aroused to fear and love and to be saddened and to rejoice - what does this accomplish? "You have defiled the land of the peoples," and you have defiled body and soul - these are the screens that separate between us and our Father in Heaven, and our eyes have grown dim from seeing what is above in order to become aroused. For the man who becomes aroused about something suddenly, whether to joy or to sadness, this is because, although he himself does not see it, his own fortune sees (Megillah 3a) what has been decreed upon him from above or upon his relatives. And likewise, at a time of service, sometimes a person is aroused to serve his service completely, at a time of gladness with gladness, and at a time of sadness with sadness, and this is because on that day or at that hour he has some merit hanging over him, and what is above is revealed to him.
Pele Yoetz 158:2: And since purity of the body causes purity of the soul, behold, therefore, it is fitting to be very careful with purity of the body, perhaps he can be strengthened in Torah and fear and love and joy and complete service. And if, through purity, he gains anything at all in the service of the Creator, it is enough for a person to trouble himself a thousand thousand troubles and to spend many expenses for this. And therefore let him not refrain, for anything at all, from immersing in a purifying mikveh - whatever he can do for the sake of repentance, to purify the defilement of his own sins, and especially to purify himself from his own impurity if he has been defiled by anything - let him not fail to do so, for he shall be called pure, pure. The Holy One, blessed be He, is pure, and His servants are pure, and whoever serves the LORD in purity, behold, his reward is doubled good.
Pele Yoetz 158:3: And it is known that impurity that comes forth from a person's own body is severe, and therefore let a man muster his strength to immerse for a seminal emission - that is, when he has had marital relations - and all the more so, a fortiori, if he had a seminal emission involuntarily, in which case it is fitting to be very careful and not fail to immerse, lest it be a prolonged detriment to his tranquility. And the disciples of the Ari, of blessed memory, have already written that whoever has had a seminal emission, God forbid, if he immerses immediately that same day and returns to the LORD, He shall have mercy on him and erase the destructive force created from the sin of his emission. And who is the man who would not have mercy on his own soul and hasten his own escape? And the man who fears the honored and awesome LORD shall fear and tremble to mention the awesome and revered Name of the LORD while his own impurity is still upon him, and of such a careful man it is said (I Samuel 2:30), "for those who honor Me, I shall honor."
Pele Yoetz 158:4: And we have heard a warning to immerse when going to the cemetery for a burial and the like, so that the husks and the spirit of impurity not attach themselves to him, for if he is impure, "like finds like" and is awakened. And likewise it is especially necessary to be careful, when returning from the cemetery, to immerse immediately to remove the spirit of impurity from him.
Pele Yoetz 158:5: And included in purity is that whoever has pure hands shall add strength. Let him wash his hands before every study and every prayer, and needless to say he shall be careful not to touch inside the ear or inside the nose, or a louse, or covered places during prayer, during study, and when he comes to recite a blessing or at mealtime - for even if he touched only the tip of one finger, his hands have become impure and he is obligated in washing of the hands, as the Sages have said, and he should not transgress the words of the Sages in a light matter, for his punishment shall be greater precisely because of the lightness of the matter. And it is especially necessary to be careful in a place where there is no lack of purse and no great trouble, for God shall be angry at his own voice and destroy the work of his hands, and his prayer is torn from him, and wisdom is turned away from him. And likewise one must be careful with the purity of garments, that there be no dirt or filth of excrement, or urine, or semen on them, and one must warn adults to be careful with children, that they wipe them well so that the LORD's desire prosper in their hands and they merit the crown of Torah. And likewise adults must be careful with wiping in that place. And I praise the custom of those who practice wiping with water, which cleans well, but those who wipe with paper or with a rag, I am concerned that they cannot clean well. And it is known that excrement at the opening of the anus is a hindrance to everyone, even the smallest amount, and his prayer is an abomination, God forbid (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim, siman 76:5).
Pele Yoetz 158:6: And likewise one must be careful with the purity of the place where he prays or studies or recites a blessing, that it be clean and free of any excrement or urine, and it is especially necessary to be careful in a place where there are small children - let him stand guard and examine well, well, and be careful and alert not to enter, God forbid, into the category of "for he has despised the word of the LORD," and so on (Numbers 15:31), and the category of "and those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed" (I Samuel 2:30), and his prayer, his study, and his blessings shall be an abomination, God forbid. And this warning rests upon the woman more than the man, and every man shall warn his wife about this, and in all such matters, day by day let him utter speech and inform of its severity, so that they keep and so that they do.
Pele Yoetz 158:7: And likewise one must be careful with the purity of his own body, that it not be a vessel full of excrement, and he should not fail to examine himself every morning and at every time he needs to, for it is known that whoever delays relieving himself transgresses "you shall not make your souls detestable" (Makkot 16b). We thus learn that he defiles his own soul. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Ta'anit 11a): a person should always regard himself as though a holy presence dwells within his own bowels, as it is said (Hosea 11:9), "the Holy One is in your midst." And they said in the Holy Zohar that just as the Shechinah rests upon him, he must be careful with the purity of his own person and the purity of his own dwelling. And it is obvious, for the God who is revered in the great and awesome council of the holy ones shall draw near only to the man who is pure. And one mitzvah draws another, for whoever comes to purify himself with the purity of his body and his garments is assisted from Heaven to understand and comprehend the Torah and to serve his service with complete service, and to fear and love the honored and awesome LORD with pure fear of the LORD.
Pele Yoetz 158:8: And if purity in the mikveh is always good, all the more so on the eves of Sabbaths and festivals and the eve of Rosh Chodesh, when one must make preparation and be a vessel ready to receive illumination and additional holiness that descends below on these days, and from the splendor of their abundance holiness shall be drawn upon his soul, spirit, and neshamah, and their illumination shall remain for all the days. And we have heard a warning from the disciples of the Ari, of blessed memory, to immerse also on the morning of the holy Sabbath, for there is an addition of nefesh, ruach, and neshamah from the aspect of the Sabbath day. And they said that the man who was not pure and does not immerse, the additional nefesh, ruach, and neshamah shall not descend upon him. And who has heard such a thing and would not gird strength to immerse, and not transgress, so as not to lose much good - only if he is prevented by circumstances beyond his control, which the Merciful One exempts.
Pele Yoetz 159:1: Letter Yud: Fear - Fear is no small matter, for guarding against everything evil depends on it. And it is known that there is fear and there is fear - one is called external fear, that one fears punishments in this world and the World to Come, for many are the pains of the wicked and the rebukes for iniquity, to the point that a person cannot estimate in his own mind the great evil that the soul of the wicked suffers in the World to Come, to the point that they said that if a person were to have sufferings in his lifetime like the sufferings of Job, they would not be like a drop from the sea compared to the pain of the day of death, and all the pain of the day of death is not like a drop from the sea compared to the sufferings of the World to Come, which give the wicked strength to bear them - and those who pass through the Valley of Weeping, He makes it a place of springs (Psalms 84:7). And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Eruvin 19a) that they cause rivers of tears to flow. Behold, therefore, a person, while he is still young, must have mercy on his own soul and reckon the reward of a transgression against its loss, and believe with complete faith that the Holy One, blessed be He, is not lenient and does not forgive even the smallest amount.
Pele Yoetz 159:2: And a certain soul has already revealed to the holy Rabbi, the author of Reshit Chokhmah, that they are exacting with a person from Heaven much more than he thinks, and God shall bring everything into judgment. Therefore the man who is fearful and tenderhearted shall be careful and guard against every sin as against a sword, and if he sins, let him hasten his own escape, before the days of evil come and days when regret shall not help, and while he still has strength, let him do whatever is in his power to do. However, this fear is called in the Holy Zohar "bad fear," for it turns out that he does not fear the LORD but fears for his own soul - and even so, this fear too is good, for from not for its own sake he comes to for its own sake. However, pure fear of the LORD is that he fear the fear of exaltedness, because He is great and dominant, and so on, for great is the LORD, and to His greatness and the perfection of His attributes and His knowledge there is no fathoming and no number. And not every person merits this fear, but everything depends on a person's own arousal and on his deeds, and on his diligence in studying books that teach a person knowledge and fear of the LORD.
Pele Yoetz 159:3: And the great essential for everything in holiness is striving and diligence. And it is known that the mitzvah to fear the honored and awesome LORD is one of the 613 mitzvot, and it is great, and it is a constant mitzvah - for at every time and moment that he remembers to fear the LORD, he fulfills a Torah-mandated mitzvah. And this is one of the things a person can never say, at any moment, that he wished to fulfill the mitzvah but could not, for there are mitzvot that depend on thought and remembrance, which it suffices to fulfill constantly - while sitting in his house and while walking on the road and while in the company of people, or occupied with his business and sitting in his shop, and the like, let him not turn his mind to idleness, but shall think pure thoughts, and through this he fulfills mitzvot, and the Holy One, blessed be He, establishes for him a reward.
Pele Yoetz 159:4: And how good it would be for him to have it constantly in his mouth to say, from time to time, the verse "I have set the LORD always before me" (Psalms 16:8). And let him picture the Name before his eyes, vocalized with the vocalization of fear or the vocalization of Shechinah, for so did they write in the name of the Ari, of blessed memory, that it is effective for fear. (And I have seen men of deeds who would write on parchment or on paper these three words: "YHVH," "ahavah" [love], "yirah" [fear], and would bind it beneath their fingers in a manner that it would not be seen outside, to be a remembrance between their eyes always while sitting in their house and while walking on the road.) And behold, this mitzvah of fear brings its own companions along with it, for through it one is guarded from everything evil. And happy is the man who is always fearful, lest, God forbid, he cause distress and anger to the exalted King, awesome and terrible - let the man tremble and be seized, and turn away from evil and do good to give peace of mind to his Former.
Pele Yoetz 160:1: Knowledge - How much knowledge there is, that even if a man were to live as many years as twice Elijah's, he would not suffice to know one part in a thousand of what there is to know. And it is known that they punish in Heaven for what a person could have known and did not strive to know, and they ask him on the day of judgment also about the Account of the Chariot and about the secrets of the Torah. And they said in the Holy Zohar that whoever does not know the secrets of the Torah is ashamed in the World to Come. And they said: whoever did not enter and exit [the depths of Torah study], better for him that he had not been created. And certainly the Holy One, blessed be He, does not deal tyrannically with His creatures, and everything depends on what he could have learned. However, it is fitting for a person to give precedence to what is most needed first - such as the practical laws and books of ethics and fear of the LORD and the order of service - and afterward, he shall go on and strive, day by day, to acquire new knowledge, what he did not know yesterday or the day before, and acquire completeness for his own soul, and not waste precious time that he could use to acquire knowledge - let him not spend it in vain.
Pele Yoetz 160:2: And the halachic authorities have already written that whoever can engage in wise dialectics and acquire new knowledge, and spends the time studying Psalms and Zohar and the like, is considered, relative to himself, as neglecting Torah - all the more so, a fortiori, if he occupies himself with idle matters when it is in his power to acquire knowledge of Torah and mitzvot, his punishment shall certainly be greater than one who cannot acquire it, either due to lack of knowledge or lack of someone to teach him, for certainly the man who can find someone to teach him is not exempted on the day of judgment by his lack of knowledge, for he should have gone to a sage to teach him. And we have already learned (Avot 4:1): who is wise? He who learns from every person. And even if he did not study in his youth, his hope is not lost and his prospect is not void, for he can study even in his old age, and "he who walks with the wise shall become wise" (Proverbs 13:20). And he should not be ashamed or embarrassed to ask.
Pele Yoetz 160:3: And whoever the LORD has graced with understanding shall not withhold good and shall not be ashamed to teach understanding to the people who seek the LORD, and shall be sought out even without being asked, and found without being sought, and when he stands in the company of men, he shall strive to draw the conversation toward words of ethics and tell them the way they should walk and the deeds they should do. Happy is the man who has found wisdom, and the man who imparts understanding to others - behold, his reward is very great, for he gives great peace of mind to his Former, as explained in the Holy Zohar regarding the virtue of one who brings merit to another - wonder upon wonder.
Pele Yoetz 161:1: Inclination - Every person has two inclinations, the good inclination and the evil inclination. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 61b): the wicked, the evil inclination judges them; the righteous, the good inclination judges them; the intermediate, this one and that one judge them. This means to say that the righteous man, regarding a matter he is already accustomed to, the good inclination rules over him to the point that his soul does not desire to do evil. And the wicked, since they have transgressed transgressions and have become accustomed to them, it has become to them as permitted, so that they do not strive to do a good thing and do not withdraw their hand from doing every evil, and their soul does not desire to do so, for the way of a fool is straight in his own eyes, and he goes from evil to evil and desires when the transgression will come to his hand, since it is not considered a transgression in his eyes.
Pele Yoetz 161:2: But the intermediate, this one and that one judge him - that is, his own flesh grieves over him for doing the transgression, but his inclination overpowers him until he transgresses against his own mind and the mind of his Maker. And of such cases our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 5a): a person should always incite the good inclination against the evil inclination - meaning, through pure thoughts, that the living take to heart sufficient arguments, for there are indeed many and many arguments to prove straightforwardly that it is fitting for a person to run to every mitzvah and flee from transgression. If he overcomes it, good; and if not, that his own mind cannot grasp the sufficient arguments there are to push away his evil inclination, let him engage in Torah, in books of ethics, and when he sets his heart to study or hear teachings with the intention of acting upon them, the words of ethics pierce the heart to its innermost chamber, and if the evil inclination is stone, it dissolves, and if it is iron, it shatters. If he overcomes it, good; and if not, that the desire for the transgression has overpowered him greatly and he cannot subdue his inclination to separate from it, let him recite the Shema, and it shall seem in his own eyes that an obligation rests upon a person to give over his own soul for "sanctify the LORD" for the honor of the LORD. And if it is light in his eyes to give over his own soul to death, all the more so shall he bear subduing his own inclination, and according to the pain is the reward. If he overcomes it, good; and if not, that he thinks, "I shall sin and repent," and "there is yet time appointed," and "I shall taste the taste of transgression and rejoice in my youth and repent in my old age" - for this let the day of death be remembered to him, for death does not delay, and for him specifically, that death may come upon him first, for whoever says, "I shall sin and repent," is not given the means to repent (Yoma 85b), and through this he can be saved from his inclination. And all the trouble is at the beginning, for beginnings are difficult, until he becomes accustomed and enters into the category of righteous regarding that matter, at which point the good inclination judges him and his soul does not desire to do evil.
Pele Yoetz 161:3: However, all this benefits an intermediate person, but the wicked, whom the evil inclination judges, have almost lost their hope and their prospect is void. And there is no wicked man who is truly, fully wicked, and no righteous man who is truly, fully righteous, and no intermediate man who is truly, fully intermediate - rather, whoever is accustomed to doing some good thing and withdrawing his hand from some evil thing, to the point that the evil inclination does not entice him regarding that matter, he is righteous regarding that matter. And all the transgressions that a person tramples underfoot until they become to him as permitted, and his heart does not grieve over them - such as looking at women and hearing forbidden speech, and deception, and mentioning the Name in vain and false and vain oaths in the languages of the gentiles, and neglecting communal prayers, and evil speech and mockery and vulgar speech, and many, many kinds of forbidden things, and sins and transgressions, and neglect of Torah at times of leisure, worse than all of them - woe to a generation in whose days this has come to pass, that there are many, many among the multitude of the people who stumble into all these, or some of them, or more than these, and have trampled them so much that they have become to them as fully permitted, in a manner that if they see a God-fearing man who wishes to be careful not to do these things and wishes to walk in the way of the good, they call him "pious" or "hypocrite" as a mockery. Woe to those who do these things, for they sin and cause others to sin and prevent the many from walking in the way of the good, and this is because these and similar severe prohibitions seem to them like a matter of piety, and they say, "not every person can be pious like the sage."
Pele Yoetz 161:4: And these, upon hearing that it is a severe prohibition, explicit in Mishnah, Gemara, and Shulchan Aruch - such as what we learned (Avot 3:2): two who sit together and there are no words of Torah between them, this is a session of scoffers. And what we learned (ibid. 1:5): whoever converses excessively with a woman causes evil to himself, neglects words of Torah, and in the end inherits Gehinnom. And likewise we learned (ibid. 4:21): jealousy, desire, and honor remove a person from the world. And many such things whose prohibition and severity are explicit in Pirkei Avot, which they sing in the synagogue - and everything the sages preach to the multitude of the people is not matters of piety but matters of prohibition, whose prohibition is explicit in the words of our holy Rabbis in the Talmud and the halachic authorities. And if, upon hearing them, they were to take it to heart to regret the evil and turn from their evil way, it would be good, but the difficulty is that after hearing them, there are many who do not abandon their bad custom, and the world conducts itself as is its custom. Woe to people for the day of judgment and the day of rebuke. And if a man is careful, righteous, and upright in all his ways, but is not careful at all in one matter, which has become to him as permitted, he shall be called wicked with regard to that matter. And greater than this, our teacher Yonah wrote (Sha'arei Teshuvah, gate 1, section 6) that whoever is not careful even in only one matter, and it has become to him as permitted, is called an apostate with regard to that matter, and is counted among the transgressors - for if the servant were to say to his master, "whatever you tell me I shall do, except for this matter," this is rebellion against the kingdom. In a manner that in this orphaned generation, almost the greatest of the great can say with a full mouth, "I know of myself that I am wicked, exceedingly wicked, before the Omnipresent," for there is almost no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin in one matter of prohibition or a bad trait that has become to him as permitted.
Pele Yoetz 161:5: And well did the early sages Abaye and Rava say, "we are like intermediates" (Berachot 61b) - meaning, that whoever's soul desires evil, even though he subdues his inclination, is called an "intermediate," this one and that one judging him. And there are two kinds of intermediates: there is an intermediate whose evil inclination ultimately defeats him and leads him astray from the mind of his Maker, and there is an intermediate who is mighty, subduing his inclination - and this is the whole of man: that whatever he knows to be forbidden and shameful, he shall strive with all vigor and might to change his bad custom and walk in the ways of the good. So shall the man act who has regard for the honor of his Maker and for his own spirit and soul, and whatever a man desires he can do when he wishes - nothing is withheld from him, and whoever comes to purify himself is assisted (Shabbat 104a, Yoma 38b).
Pele Yoetz 162:1: Superiority - This is a bad trait, that a person desires to have superiority over his fellow - and not only in worldly matters is this a bad trait, which consumes from soul to flesh, for he is never happy with his own portion, and stumbles into the trait of jealousy, desire, and honor, which remove a person from the world, and all his days are pains, for he continually pines over his fellow's good fortune and attainment of honor, which he himself cannot attain, and he toils to grow rich and attain what he cannot attain, and it turns out that the days he lives on earth are lived in pain, and his end shall be disgraceful. But even in matters of Heaven, if he performs mitzvot and good deeds in order to rise in levels and surpass his fellow, this too is a bad illness, and the Holy Zohar calls such people the "mixed multitude," of whom it is written (Genesis 6:4), "these were the mighty men who were of old, men of renown" - and from this he grieves when he sees his fellow rising in levels, and he wishes that all be lower than himself. And when he sees one who is deficient in the service of the LORD, his heart rejoices that he himself remains above, in his own opinion, while his fellow remains below - and this is a great evil, for if regarding one who rejoices at his fellow's downfall in worldly matters it is written (Proverbs 17:5), "and he who rejoices at calamity shall not go unpunished," all the more so, a fortiori, one who rejoices at his fellow's deficient attainment and at his angering his Creator, for it turns out that he hates his Creator and desires His distress - may the Merciful One save us from this mindset. And also, because he has this bad trait, upon hearing someone praised for his wisdom and his deeds, his own flesh grieves over him, but upon hearing someone disparaged, he has peace of mind, and he too searches to find fault with the holy, and many such evils follow from this bad trait.
Pele Yoetz 162:2: And granted it is written (Proverbs 23:17), "let your heart not envy sinners, but rather fear the LORD all the day," and it is written (Genesis 30:1), "and Rachel envied her sister," and they said (Bava Batra 21a): the envy of scribes increases wisdom - this refers to the matter of desiring, oneself too, to rise in levels. And every person is obligated to say, "when shall my deeds reach the deeds of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob?" (Tanna D'vei Eliyahu Rabbah, ch. 25) - not in order to resemble them and not for glory and praise and not on condition of receiving a reward, but only to give peace of mind to his Former specifically. And the man who is pure, whose entire aim and desire is to give peace of mind to his Former specifically, let the servant say, "would that all the LORD's people were prophets" (Numbers 11:29), for the LORD shall put His spirit, a proper spirit, within them, that they grow wise in Torah and increase and greatly magnify good deeds. And if I am not worthy of this because I have sinned, and the good is withheld from me - for these are the screens that separate between me and my Father in Heaven, God forbid - at least let there be others who give peace of mind to my Father in Heaven; the good shall come from any source. And if it is fitting before Him, blessed be His Name, to give my fellow more than me according to his deeds or according to the wonders of one of perfect understanding, is it not all the more so fitting before me? Rather, I shall strive with all my strength to give peace of mind to my Former from whatever comes to my hand, and He shall do what is good in His eyes. And all the more so regarding worldly matters, for all superiorities are vanity and vexation of spirit, and what advantage does a person have from all his labor, that he labors to attain wealth or honor? Vanity of vanities, all is vanity, for whoever has even a little brain in his skull. And truly they said (Avot 4:1): who is rich? He who is happy with his portion - and he is good-hearted always and with every person in love and affection. Happy is he in this world, and it is good for him in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 163:1: Descent - It is good for a man to go down rather than go up. Regarding the matter of a seat, King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 25:7), "better that they say to you, come up here, than that you be put lower before a noble." Not that he should sit very low, but rather, after he recognizes the place fitting for him according to his own understanding, let him sit a little lower. And likewise regarding the matter of marriage, our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Yevamot 63a): descend a step, take a wife. Only if he is a poor man and they give him a great deal quickly and a gift, in a manner that he shall have settlement and ease to serve the LORD and stand guard over Torah and over service, then if he wishes to take a wife from a place of the great, he has lost nothing.
Pele Yoetz 163:2: And a person shall always choose to sit with those greater and better than himself, so that he can learn from them, even though he himself shall be lower, and he should not choose to sit in a place where there are no [worthy] men, even though he would then rise higher. And as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avot 4:15[?]): be a tail to lions and not a head to foxes. And they gave a sign for this: the tail of the lion is, after all, still the body of a lion, while the head of the fox is a fox. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Yevamot 63a): descend a step and take a groomsman [companion]. And they said (Avot 1:4): let yourself be covered in the dust of the feet of the sages and drink their words thirstily. And "man looks to the eyes" (I Samuel 16:7) - regarding a rabbi, that every time he goes to sages greater than himself, he grows wise and learns what he did not know, and this is the whole of man. And also, whoever wishes to be exalted shall descend, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Eruvin 54a): "and from the wilderness, a gift" (Numbers 21:18) - if a person makes himself like a wilderness, the Torah is given to him as a gift, and they inherited it from God, and he rises to magnify it. And it is fitting for a person to lower himself like hyssop for the honor of his Maker - such as learning from every person and honoring the poor, to gladden the hearts of the wretched and revive the hearts of the downtrodden, and to be a seeker of peace, loving people and drawing them near to the Torah, and greeting every person first. And let him not say, "I am a great man, and it is not befitting my honor to lower myself before so-and-so," for this is his own honor: that he honor his Maker with what He has graced him, and through this he shall find favor and good sense in the eyes of God and man. Whoever does these things is exalted - he shall surely rise.
Pele Yoetz 164:1: Despair - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avot 1:7): do not despair of retribution - for one must always have before his eyes that he is destined for all kinds of calamities that stir to come into the world, and that he is willing to accept the decree of Heaven with love, in a manner that nothing come upon him suddenly, so that he not grow weary of rebuke, and not lose his mind when the days of evil come upon him, but rather accept everything with affection as is fitting to accept the decrees of our Father in Heaven, who is master of His world to do in it as He wishes, and we are His servants and the flock of His hand - for everything we are obligated to thank and bless Him. And through this too, he shall come to fulfill the verse (Ecclesiastes 7:14), "in the day of good fortune be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider" - which the commentators explained to mean: in the day of good fortune, be in the good way, because in the day of good fortune he considers the day of adversity that he is destined to face, and prepares for himself the path he should walk before the days of evil come.
Pele Yoetz 164:2: And all the more so must one not despair regarding the day of death, for the day of death is destined for him from the day of his birth, and death does not delay, and there is none saved from it, and let him always repent today lest he die tomorrow, and let all his accounts and all his affairs be written and clearly explained, for one must be concerned lest he die suddenly. Even if he is a young man like the cedars, who can guarantee that he shall not die in his youth? Of this it is said (Proverbs 28:14), "happy is the man who is always fearful" - for through this he shall prepare provisions for his journey and strive to complete his obligation, and shall command his sons and his household, and his rest shall be in peace. And likewise regarding good fortune, our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 10a): even if a sharp sword is laid upon a person's neck, let him not despair of mercy. And "whoever trusts in the LORD, kindness shall surround him" (Psalms 32:10). And all the more so, a fortiori, regarding the redemption, an obligation rests upon us to sit and wait, as it is written (Habakkuk 2:3), "though it tarry, wait for it, for it shall surely come with joy" - so may it be His will, speedily in our days, Amen.
Pele Yoetz 165:1: Toil - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Megillah 6b): if a person says to you, "I have labored and not found," do not believe him; and if a person says to you, "I have not labored and I have found," do not believe him. And man was not created in this world except to enjoy in the World to Come the fruit of his own labor. And "man is born to toil" - happy is he whose toil is in Torah and good deeds, to subdue his own inclination, to fulfill every good thing and withdraw his hand from doing every evil. According to the toil, the labor, and the trouble, so does he give peace of mind to his Former, and according to the pain is the reward. And man was not created in this world to eat to satiety and rejoice in human pleasures, which are the plagues of men for the World to Come, but rather to trouble himself with great trouble, day and night, without sitting idle, to serve his own service, the service of a servant, in thought, speech, and deed, according to the camel is the burden (Ketubot 67a). "He who adds knowledge adds sorrow" (Ecclesiastes 1:18) over what he should have done and did not do.
Pele Yoetz 165:2: And of this they said (Yalkut Shimoni, Toldot, 111) that Jacob and Esau divided the worlds - Esau took this world, and Jacob took the World to Come. And the commentators raised a difficulty, for our eyes see that when Israel dwelt on its own land, they were... satisfied and full of the LORD's blessing, each man under his vine and under his fig tree, and even now the LORD shall not abandon His people, and there are exceedingly wealthy men who have houses full of every good thing, and wealth and honor - and from where did they merit this, if this world belongs to Esau? And many answers have been given to this matter, and what I see, according to the truth, is that Jacob did not receive his portion in these things, for all the good things of this world diminish into vanity, since a person finds no tranquility of spirit, and eats the bread of sorrows while standing guard over Torah and over service, and cannot enjoy what he has, and must always be frugal and content with the necessary minimum for his own life, for his own need, so that he can serve the LORD, and shall consecrate the rest to the LORD to perform mitzvot and good deeds. And he cannot sleep all night as he wishes, but rather his eyes precede the watches. And all the more so if the arrogant waters have passed over his head, the sins of youth - all his days are pains, and he must afflict and mortify his own soul as much as he can bear. And after all the toil and trouble, he must always be fearful lest he has not done what he should have done, and "he who adds knowledge adds sorrow" (Ecclesiastes 1:18) upon himself and upon his offspring and upon all the seed of the house of Israel, and his own flesh grieves over him, and his own soul mourns over him for the honor of Heaven and the distress of Heaven, in a manner that the Israelite man who walks in the ways of the LORD has no rest in this world and does not enjoy it even with his little finger, as our holy teacher said (Ketubot 104a), and all his days in this world are spent in grief and sighing and great toil, until he goes to his end and rests in proper rest - there the weary in strength shall rest, and he shall find rest. Then Israel shall rejoice in its Maker, and eat the fruit of his deeds.
